source_text: Nunc ad diuina testimonia transeamus. sed prius unum proferam, quod est simile diuino et ob nimiam uetustatem et quod is quem nominabo ex hominibus in deos relatus est.. apud Ciceronem U. Cotta pontifex disputans contra Stoicos de religionibus et uarietate opinionum quae solent esse de diis, ut more Academicorum omnia faceret incerta, quinque fuisse Mercurios ait et enumeratis per ordinem quattuor quintum fuisse eum a quo sit Argus occisus; ob eamque causam in Aegyptum profugisse atque Aegyptiis leges ac litteras tradidisse. hunc Aegyptii Thoyth appellant, a quo apud eos primus anni sui mensis id est September nomen accepit. idem oppidum condidit, quod etiam nunc graece uocatur Mercurii ciuitas, et Pheneatae colunt eum religiose. qui tametsi homo fuit, antiquissimus tamen et instructissimus omni genere doctrinae adeo, ut ei multarum rerum et artium scientia Trismegisto cognomen inponeret. hic scripsit libros et quidem multos ad cognitionem diuinarum rerum pertinentes, in quibus maiestatem summi ac singularis dei asserit isdemque nominibus appellat quibus nos dominum et patrem. ac ne quis nomen eius requireret, άνώνυμον esse dixit, eo quod nominis proprietate non egeat, ob ipsam scilicet unitatem. ipsius haec uerba sunt: o se Oso; είς, b δὲ είς όνόματος ou προσδέεται έστι ykp o wv ὰνώνυμος. deo igitur nomen (non) est, quia solus est, nec opus est proprio uocabulo, nisi cum discrimen exigit multitudo, ut unam quamque personam sua nota et appellatione designes. deo autem, quia semper unus est, proprium nomen est deus. Superest de responsis sacrisque carminibus testimonia quae sunt multo certiora proferre. nam fortasse ii contra quos agimus nec poetis putent esse credendum tamquam uana fingentibus nec philosophis, quod errare potuerint, quia et ipsi homines fuerint. M. Varro, quo nemo umquam doctior ne apud Graecos quidem uixit, in libris rerum diuinarum quos ad C. Caesarem pontificem maximum scripsit, cum de quindecimuiris loqueretur, Sibyllinos libros ait non fuisse unius Sibyllae, sed appellari uno nomine Sibyllinos, quod omnes feminae uates Sibyllae sint a ueteribus nuncupatae uel ab unius Delphidis nomine uel a consiliis deorum enuntiandis. atouq enim deos, non Osouc, et consilium non βουλήν, sed βούλλαν appellabant Aeolico genere sermonis. itaque Sibyllam dictam esse quasi θεοβούλην. ceterum Sibyllas decem numero fuisse, easque omnes enumerauit sub auctoribus qui de singulis scriptitauerint. primam fuisse de Persis, cuius mentionem fecerit Nicanor, qui res gestas Alexandri Macedonis scripsit; secundam Libyssam, cuius meminerit Euripides in Lamiae prologo; tertiam Delphida, de qua Chrysippus loquatur in eo libro quem de diuinatione conposuit; quartam Cimmeriam in Italia, quam Naeuius in libris belli Punici, Piso in annalibus nominet; quintam Erythraeam, quam Apollodorus Erythraeus adfirmet suam fuisse ciuem eamque Grais Ilium petentibus uaticinatam et perituram esse Troiam et Homerum mendacia scripturum; sextam Samiam, de qua scribat Eratosthenes in antiquis annalibus Samiorum repperisse so scriptum; septimam Cumanam nomine Amaltheam, quae ab aliis Herophile uel Demophile nominetur, eamque nouem libros attulisse ad regem Tarquinium Priscum ac pro iis trecentos philippeos postulasse regemque aspernatum pretii magnitudinem derisisse mulieris insaniam; illam in conspectu regis tris combussisse ac pro reliquis idem pretium poposcisse; Tarquinium multo magis insanire mulierem putauisse; quae denuo tribus aliis exustis cum in eodem pretio perseueraret, motum esse regem ac residuos trecentis aureis emisse; quorum postea numerus sit auctus, Capitolio refecto, quod ex omnibus ciuitatibus et Italicis et Graecis praecipueque Erythraeis coacti adlatique sunt Romam cuiuscumque Sibyllae nomine fuerunt; octauam Hellespontiam in agro Troiano natam, uico Marmesso circa oppidum Gergithium, quam scribat Heraclides Ponticus Solonis et Cyri fuisse temporibus; nonam Phrygiam, quae uaticinata sit Ancyrae; decimam Tiburtem nomine Albuneam, quae Tiburi colatur ut dea iuxta ripas amnis Anienis, cuius in gurgite simulacrum eius inuentum esse dicitur tenens in manu librum. arum onmium Sibyllarum carmina et teruntur et habentur, praeterquam Cymaeae, cuius libri a Romanis occultantur nec eos ab ullo nisi a quindecimuiris inspici fas habent. et sunt singularum singuli libri: quos, quia Sibyllae nomine inscribuntur, unius esse credunt, suntque confusi nec discerni ac suum cuique adsignari potest nisi Erythraeae, quae et nomen suum uerum carmini inseruit et Erythraeam se nominatuiri praelocuta est, cum esset orta Babylone. sed et IlOS confuse Sibyllam dicemus, sicubi testimoniis earum ruent abutendum. omnes igitur hae Sibyllae unum deum praedicant, maxime tamen Erythraea, quae celebrior inter ceteras ac nobilior habetur, siquidem Fenestella diligentissimus scriptor de quindecim uiris dicens ait restituto Capitolio rettulisse ad senatum C. Curionem consulem, ut legati Erythras mitterentur, qui carmina Sibyllae conquisita Romam deportarent: itaque missos esse P. Gabinium M. Otacilium L. Valerium, qui descriptos a priuatis uersus circa mille Romam deportarunt. idem dixisse Varronem supra ostendimus. in his ergo uersibus quos Romam legati adtulerunt de uno deo haec sunt testimonia: εἷς θεός, ὂς μόνος ἄρχει, ὐπερμεγέθης ἀγένητος. hunc esse solum summum deum, qui caelum fecerit luminibusque distinxerit: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μόνος εἶς πανυπέρτατος, ὃς πεποίηκεν οὐρανὸν ἡέλιὸν τε καὶ ἀστέρας, ἠδέ σελήνην, καρποφόρον γαῖαν τε καὶ ὕδατος οἴδματα πόντου. qui quoniam solus sit aedificator mundi et artifex rerum uel quibus constat uel quae in eo sunt, solum coli oportere testatur: αὐτὸν τὸν μόνον ὄντα σέβεσθ᾽ ἡγήτορα κόσμου. ὃς μόνος εἰς αἰῶνα καὶ ἐξ αἰῶνος ἐτύχθη. item alia Sibylla quaecumque est cum perferre se ad homines uocem dei diceret, sic ait: μοῦνος γὰρ θεὸς εἰμὶ καὶ οὐκ ἔστι θεὸς ἄλλος. Exequerer nunc testimonia ceterarum, nisi et haec sufticerent et illa opportunioribus locis reseruarem. sed cum defendamus causam ueritatis aput eos qui aberrantes a ueritate falsis religionibus seruiunt, quod genus probationis aduersus eos magis adhibere debemus quam ut eos deorum suorum testimoniis reuincamus?
pass_a_gloss: Now let us proceed to divine testimonies. But first, I will bring forth one thing, which is similar to the divine and, because of its great antiquity, and because the one I will name, having been a man, was related to the gods. In Cicero, U. Cotta, a pontiff, arguing against the Stoics about religions and the variety of opinions that are usually held about the gods, so that, in the manner of the Academics, he might make all things uncertain, says that there were five Mercurys and, having enumerated four in order, says that the fifth was the one by whom Argus was killed; and because of this cause, he fled to Egypt and handed over laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call this one Thoyth, from whom, among them, the first month of the year, that is, September, received its name. This same one founded a city, which is even now called, in Greek, the city of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Who, although he was a man, was nevertheless most ancient and most instructed in every kind of doctrine, so that he was given the surname Trismegistus, because of his knowledge of many things and arts. This one wrote books, and indeed many, pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and calls him by the same names by which we call the Lord and Father. And lest anyone should seek his name, he said that it is anonymous, because it does not need the property of a name, on account of its unity. These are his words: 'O se Oso; one, indeed, one, not having a need for a name, is anonymous.' Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone, nor is there a need for a proper word, unless when a multitude demands a distinction, so that you might designate each person by their own mark and appellation. But for God, because he is always one, 'God' is his proper name. It remains to bring forth testimonies that are much more certain from the sacred and prophetic writings. For perhaps those against whom we are arguing do not think that poets should be believed, as if they were inventing vain things, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, since they also were men. M. Varro, than whom no one was ever more learned, not even among the Greeks, in the books of divine things that he wrote to C. Caesar, the pontifex maximus, when he was speaking about the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not of one Sibyl, but were called by one name, Sibylline, because all the female prophets were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the counsels of the gods that were to be announced. For they called the gods not 'Osouc', but 'theos', and counsel not 'βουλήν', but 'βούλλαν', in the Aeolic kind of speech. And so, the Sibyl was said to be, as it were, 'θεοβούλην'. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and he enumerated all of them, under the authors who wrote about each one. The first was from Persia, whom Nicanor mentioned, who wrote about the deeds of Alexander of Macedon; the second was Libyssa, whom Euripides remembered in the prologue of Lamia; the third was Delphid, about whom Chrysippus spoke in that book that he composed about divination; the fourth was Cimmerian, in Italy, whom Naevius named in the books of the Punic war, and Piso in the annals; the fifth was Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed to be his fellow citizen, and who prophesied to the Greeks, when they were going to Ilium, that Troy would be destroyed, and that Homer would write falsehoods; the sixth was Samian, about whom Eratosthenes wrote in the ancient annals of the Samians; the seventh was Cumana, named Amalthea, who was also called Herophile or Demophile by others, and who brought nine books to king Tarquin the Elder, and asked for three hundred philippeos for them, and the king, despising the magnitude of the price, ridiculed the woman's insanity; she, in the presence of the king, burned three of them, and asked for the same price for the remaining ones; Tarquin, thinking that the woman was even more insane, was moved, and bought the remaining ones for three hundred gold pieces; the number of which was later increased, when the Capitol was rebuilt, and they were brought from all the cities, both Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, to Rome, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were; the eighth was Hellespontian, born in the Trojan field, in the village of Marmesso, near the city of Gergithium, whom Heraclides of Pontus wrote was contemporary with Solon and Cyrus; the ninth was Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra; the tenth was Tiburtine, named Albunea, who is worshiped as a goddess at Tibur, near the banks of the river Anio, and whose image is said to have been found in the whirlpool, holding a book in her hand. And the songs of all the Sibyls are both corrupted and preserved, except for those of the Cumana, whose books are hidden by the Romans, and it is not lawful for anyone to inspect them, except for the quindecimvirs. And there are individual books of each one: which, because they are inscribed with the name of the Sibyl, are believed to be of one Sibyl, and are confused, and cannot be discerned, nor can each one be assigned to its own, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her song, and proclaimed that she was called Erythraean, when she was born in Babylon. But also, we will confusedly call the Sibyl, wherever we will use their testimonies. Therefore, all these Sibyls proclaim one God, especially the Erythraean, who is considered more famous and noble among the others, since Fenestella, a most diligent writer, speaking about the quindecimvirs, says that, when the Capitol was restored, C. Curio, the consul, reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae, to bring back the songs of the Sibyl that had been found; and so, P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were sent, who brought back to Rome about a thousand verses that had been written by private individuals. We showed above that Varro said the same thing. In these verses, which the legates brought to Rome, there are these testimonies about one God: 'One God, who alone rules, immense, ungenerated.' That this one is the only highest God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: 'But God alone, one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea.' Who, since he is alone the builder of the world and the artisan of things, either which consist in it or which are in it, testifies that he alone should be worshiped: 'Honor him, the only one, the leader of the world.' 'Who alone is from eternity and to eternity.' Also, another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she says that she brings the voice of God to men, says thus: 'For I am the only God, and there is no other God.' I would now bring forth the testimonies of the other Sibyls, if these were not sufficient, and if I were reserving them for more opportune places. But since we are defending the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof should we use more against them than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?
pass_b_english: We now turn to the divine testimonies. First, however, I will cite one piece of evidence that resembles the divine both because of its great antiquity and because the man I shall name was enrolled among the gods. In Cicero, the pontiff U. Cotta argues against the Stoics concerning religions and the variety of opinions usually held about the gods. He follows the Academic practice of rendering everything uncertain. He states that there were five Mercurys; after enumerating four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one who killed Argus. On that account, this figure fled to Egypt and handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoyth; from him their first month of the year—September—received its name. He also founded a city that is still called, in Greek, the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a man, he was the most ancient and the most thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many arts and sciences earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things. In them he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God, addressing him by the very names we use for the Lord and Father. Lest anyone seek his name, he declared that God is anonymous, because the divine nature has no need of a proper name on account of its unity. His own words are: "O se Oso; one, indeed, one, not needing a name, is anonymous." Therefore, God does not have a name, because he is alone; there is no need for a proper title unless a multitude requires distinction, so that each person may be designated by a unique mark and appellation. But because God is always one, "God" is his proper name.

It remains to produce testimonies from the sacred and prophetic writings that are far more certain. Perhaps those against whom we argue do not consider poets credible, since they invent fictions, nor philosophers, because they could have erred, being men themselves. M. Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks, wrote books on divine matters addressed to C. Caesar the pontifex maximus. When discussing the quindecimvirs, he states that the Sibylline books were not the work of a single Sibyl. They bear one name, "Sibylline," because the ancients called all female prophets Sibyls, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For they called the gods not "Osouc" but "theos," and counsel not "boulēn" but "boullan," in the Aeolic dialect. Hence the Sibyl was, as it were, a "theoboulēn"—a divine counsel. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and Varro enumerated them all under the authorities who wrote about each. The first was Persian, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon. The second was Libyssa, recalled by Euripides in the prologue to the Lamia. The third was the Delphid, discussed by Chrysippus in his book on divination. The fourth was Cimmerian, in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals. The fifth was the Erythraean, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirmed to be his fellow citizen; she prophesied to the Greeks bound for Ilium that Troy would fall and that Homer would write falsehoods. The sixth was Samian, recorded by Eratosthenes in the ancient annals of the Samians. The seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others. She brought nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus and demanded three hundred philippeos for them. The king scorned the high price and mocked the woman's madness. In his presence she burned three of the books and asked the same price for the remaining six. Tarquin, thinking her even more insane, was moved to buy the rest for three hundred gold pieces. The number of books later increased when the Capitol was rebuilt; volumes were collected from all cities, Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, and brought to Rome under whatever Sibyl's name they bore. The eighth was the Hellespontian, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmessa near the city of Gergithium; Heraclides of Pontus places her in the times of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the river Anio; her image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The songs of all these Sibyls are both corrupted and preserved, except those of the Cumaean. Her books the Romans keep hidden; no one but the quindecimvirs may inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are all inscribed with the name "Sibyl," they are believed to be the work of one, and are confused so that they cannot be distinguished or assigned to their proper authors—except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her verse and proclaimed herself Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. We too shall cite the Sibyls without distinction wherever their testimonies are needed.

All these Sibyls proclaim one God, above all the Erythraean, who is held more famous and noble than the rest. Fenestella, a most diligent writer on the quindecimvirs, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul C. Curio reported to the senate that legates should be sent to Erythrae to recover the Sibyl's songs. Accordingly P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were dispatched; they brought back to Rome about a thousand verses copied from private collections. We have shown above that Varro attests the same. In these verses, which the legates brought to Rome, the following testimonies concerning one God appear: "One God, who alone rules, immense, ungenerated." This is the only highest God, who made heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone, one, most high, who made heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." Because he alone is the builder of the world and the artificer of all things, whether they consist in it or are in it, he testifies that he alone ought to be worshiped: "Honor him, the only one, the leader of the world." "Who alone is from eternity and to eternity." Likewise, another Sibyl, whoever she may be, when she claims to bring the voice of God to men, declares: "For I am the only God, and there is no other God." I would now produce the testimonies of the other Sibyls, if these did not suffice and if I were not reserving them for more opportune places. But since we defend the cause of truth against those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what proof should we employ more effectively against them than to convict them by the testimonies of their own gods?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Latin text, including the Greek quotations and the detailed list of the ten Sibyls. All nuances regarding the identity of Thoyth, the nature of the name of God, and the historical accounts of the Sibylline books are preserved. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source.
